I recently replied to a job posting for a "Social Media Expert" for a real-estate manager. However, when I got there, the guy went on to explain that he needed someone to manage marketing for social media across all three of his companies, which he owns. In any case, each is a single-product company.

The company I responded to the ad for is, like I said, a real-estate manager. It's target audiences are on Facebook and Twitter. Local market, extremely low-competition, and messaging is (comparatively) casual, so would be a breeze.

The second company he seemed the most adamant about. It's a tech company whose singular product an app. The upsides are that its disruptive, in a tech field, and has low competition. There are 15 competitors. Of the top two who compete most with the company, one has been around for 16 years and the other for 12. The market is other businesses on an international level.

The third and last company is another tech company, and it too is singularly built around an app. Interestingly, the market for the app is almost identical to the market of the first company, but on an international level. Also relatively low-stress and virtually zero competition.

I suggested $46,000. His argument was that my expectations were uncomfortably high given that I would only be spending 40 hours (full-time) across all three companies and products. I countered with the fact that I would be having to address what are essentially two different markets across three different products from thee different companies, which means three times the management workload.

He asked what my expectations were for just handling the property management company and the third company. I said that because they shared such similar markets and they're both startups, I'd be willing to do $33,000, and possibly other forms of compensation. He thought this was more reasonable.

Now, I have over three years of experience in tech, and over five years experience in social media management. I've also seen a tech company through an IPO that was nearly $2 Billion. At my last job, I was paid the equivalent of just over $65,000 plus about $18,000 in stock options.

From my perspective, I'm low-balling myself-- but I'm a sucker for startups. My questions is, am I being realistic in my salary expectations?

TL;DR

  • I have over 5 years experience in social media
  • At least 3 of those years of experience in the highly-competitive tech industry
  • New job wants me to handle social media marketing for three different companies selling three different products which means three times the workload.
  • I bring with me (ethical) connections to trusted tech journalists, connections to VC, and connections to major, well-known organizations that could benefit from at least two of the companies/products.
  • I'm asking $46,000.
  • Employer is thinking more in the ballpark of low to mid $30k.

Am I being unreasonable?

I have a few questions first because, to me, the information above is informative but too broad to offer any real advice:

1. What's your location? (Country / state / region <<any of those would help)

2. What are the benefits? Clearly a startup may have some limitations but there should still be something.

3. What is their business plan for growth?

4. Have they presented an option to you where your salary grows commensurate with business expansion?

5. Are they thinking of you as a long term investment and/or need for business sustainment or is this person being shortsighted and simply thinking they need you to get the ball rolling and be done?

6. How many other employees besides the owner?

7. How long have you been unemployed?

Those may help get you a more balanced answer.

You're passionate about start-ups and that's wonderful. They have a great vibe and working environment that counts for something. Let me ask you this though, are these three products something you get excited about? Jumping to a lower salary isn't a bad thing if you truly believe this company could take off. You may want to negotiate extra time off, a 4-6 month review time period of your work with the intent of a raise, and get everything in writing.

Ultimately, if you can survive off 33k and you're happy to devote yourself to The Cause then there is no harm in taking a lower amount. If you're not passionate about the business though then not only will you not be an asset to the start-up, but you'll be unhappy after a few months on the job.

A shitty move that you could do is to accept the job and keep looking for something better. I once hired a kid who showed up to his second day of work to quit because another job offer came through.
